issues.legal_issue: An appellate court hearing an appeal against acquittal may not replace a reasonable trial-court view of the evidence with another view merely because it would have assessed the evidence differently.
material_facts: The trial court acquitted the accused after finding the prosecution evidence too weak to support conviction and identifying doubts about the time and place of the killing, the witnesses’ presence and independence, and the alleged motive.

The medical evidence showed an empty stomach and bladder and faecal matter in the large intestine, which the trial court considered consistent with the possibility that the killing occurred earlier than the prosecution claimed.

There were discrepancies about where the assault occurred and whether witnesses positioned near a drain could have seen it; the prosecution also did not establish that blood found at the site was human blood.
The trial court considered whether the deceased’s father and other witnesses might have had reasons to implicate the accused, including their relationships and a pending criminal case.
The Supreme Court found the trial court’s assessment justified and its conclusions plausible; it held that the High Court had no proper basis to substitute a different view.
issues.conclusion: The appeal was allowed, the High Court’s judgment of conviction was set aside, and the trial court’s acquittal was restored.
issues.legal_principle: In an appeal against acquittal, the appellate court must keep in view the presumption of innocence, which is reinforced by the acquittal; where two reasonable views of the evidence are possible, it should adopt the view favourable to the accused and should not interfere merely because it would have reached a different conclusion. It should also consider that the trial judge had the advantage of seeing and hearing the witnesses, and the accused is entitled to the benefit of reasonable doubt. The Court followed State of U.P. v. Samman Dass, [1972] 3 S.C.R. 58. The judgment concerns an appeal against acquittal under Section 378 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, and an appeal under Section 2 of the Supreme Court (Enlargement of Criminal Appellate Jurisdiction) Act, 1970; it also identifies Section 3 of the Evidence Act, 1872, in connection with appreciation of evidence.

rule.if: appeal_against_acquittal and trial_court_acquitted and trial_view_supported_by_evidence and evidence_permits_two_reasonable_views

predicates.appeal_against_acquittal: An appellate court is reviewing a trial court’s decision to acquit an accused.
predicates.trial_court_acquitted: The trial court acquitted the accused after assessing the evidence.
predicates.trial_view_supported_by_evidence: The evidence provides a reasonable basis for the trial court’s assessment and conclusions.
predicates.evidence_permits_two_reasonable_views: The evidence can reasonably support both the trial court’s view and a different view.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges an acquittal and the trial court’s evidence-based view is one of two reasonable views, the acquittal remains undisturbed.
